subject: giant ant
title: What If Ants Were the Size of Humans? They'd Suffocate First

scenes.text: What if ants were human-sized? They wouldn't take over. They'd suffocate before they stood up.
An ant's neck can take 5,000 times its body weight.
Scale it up and the maths flips: muscle strength grows with width squared, weight with volume cubed.
A human-sized ant would crumple under itself. Haldane said giants would break their thighs with every step.
Then air. Ants have no lungs, just tiny tubes, and anything over a quarter inch from the air starves of oxygen.
The biggest insect ever had a 71-centimetre wingspan, in an age with up to 35 percent oxygen. In our air, a giant ant can't breathe.

description:
What if ants were the size of humans? Ohio State University engineers found the neck joint of an ant can withstand 3,400 to 5,000 times its body weight, but strength scales with muscle cross-section while weight scales with volume, so a human-sized ant would likely fail under extreme loads, and as J.B.S. Haldane wrote in On Being the Right Size, giants would break their thighs every time they took a step. Insects also breathe through tracheae, tubes that deliver air by diffusion; Haldane noted anything more than a quarter inch from the air would be short of oxygen. The largest insect known, Meganeuropsis, had a wingspan of up to 71 centimetres and lived when the air held 30 to 35 percent oxygen, against 21 percent today.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Haldane's other line: drop a mouse down a mine shaft and it walks away, a horse splashes. Which animal would you scale up next?
